Hello everybody,
Lask week I posted a e-mail. Now I post the answers I have received.
Thanks a lot to the people that has answered!=20

I am assessing a wild pigeon population (Columba livia), I am using =
enough=20
transects to see pigeons, but the first times I begun to analyze the=20
populations I only saw few flocks, (between 20 to 30); they had betweeen =
140=20
to 600 pigeons. I was wondering if I could use the bootstrap procedure =
to=20
analyse the pigeons density as single instead of cluster of those first=20
pigeons. Does anyone know the answer?
Thanks a lot!



Hi,
It is probably not a good idea to perform an analysis in which each=20
individual pigeon is considered to be an object. First, the estimation=20
routines in Distance (analytical or bootstrapping) assume that the=20
probability of detecting each object is independent of all other =
objects. But=20
almost certainly you are more likely to detect an individual that is in =
a=20
group of 600 hundred than you are to detect a lone individual. Treating =
each=20
pigeon in a group is an independent object has the effect of making you=20
overestimate the mean detection distance for pigeons because big groups =
are=20
probably detectable from farther than small groups or solitaries. This =
causes=20
you to underestimate density because you are actually missing a lot more =

solitaries and small groups than the detection probability estimate is=20
telling you. You also get inappropriate confidence interval estimates on =

detection probability because your sample is not a random sample of =
possible=20
detection distances for independently detected pigeons (as the =
procedures=20
assume): you are biased towards long distances because big groups can be =

detected from further. The group size effect can be handled by treating=20
groups as objects and making group detection probability a function of =
group=20
size. But this does not get around the problem that you don't have a=20
sufficient sample size of groups to get a robust estimate of detection=20
probability. There is not much you can do about this besides collect =
more=20
data.
Sorry,
Peter Walsh

Hi Francisco,

>From what I understand of your message, you have too few observations =
from=20
your early surveys to reliably estimate a detection function and want to =

increase the apparent sample size by analyzing the individuals within a=20
cluster as if they were independent observations. Sorry, but this will =
not=20
help with your problem. The detection fitting procedure relies on the=20
observations being independent, and you cannot magically "create" new=20
independent observations. You will have a much larger apparent sample =
size,=20
but the observations will be heavily dependent on one another.

Sometimes, one is forced to analyze clustered data as individuals - for=20
example when it is hard to determine which cluster individuals are in, =
or it=20
is hard to count cluster size, or it is hard to determine the centre of =
the=20
cluster. When you are forced to do this, you have to be very careful =
when=20
selecting a model for the detection function as the model selection=20
statistics (AIC, etc) and goodness-of-fit are all compromized. All of =
these=20
assume that each observation is independent but when many observations =
come=20
from the same cluster this is not the case.

Bootstrapping will also not create independent observations - =
boostrapping is=20
something we use to get a different (and often more reliable) variance=20
estimate and confidence limits. It cannot be used to "produce" more=20
independent observations.

When you have only 20-30 observations (ie clusters) your options are:

1. Pool these observations with those from later surveys (under =
comparable=20
conditions) to estimate the detection function.

2. If you have no other data to pool with, you could try fitting some =
low-
parameter detection functions (half-normal with up to 1 adjustment; =
hazard=20
rate) and, if you have nice data with a wide shoulder and a gentle =
fall-off=20
after the shoulder, you may get a decent detection function from only =
these=20
few data. However, results may well not be reliable.

Hope this helps,

- Len Thomas

P.S. It would be helpful if you could collate all the replies you get =
and=20
post them as one message or summarize them to the distance-sampling list =
so=20
that others can read them
